questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: When Mayfair Beverages, a midsize firm raised the price of its Springfield product by 10 percent, quantity demanded fell by 25 percent. What is the price elasticity of demand (absolute value)?
questions.explanation: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, which here is 25 divided by 10, giving 2.5. Because the absolute value exceeds 1, demand is elastic: buyers are quite responsive to price. Inverting the ratio would give 0.4 and the wrong conclusion that demand is inelastic.

questions.subject: MARKETING
questions.stem: Thornbury Paints, a fast-growing firm sets the price of a new Tarrow service by estimating what customers believe it is worth, then working backward to the costs it can afford to incur. Which pricing approach is this?
questions.explanation: Value-based pricing starts with the customer's perceived worth and works backward to costs, so the price captures the value delivered. Cost-plus pricing instead adds a markup to costs, and competition-based pricing anchors on rivals' prices. Penetration pricing is a low initial price to win share, which is a different decision.

questions.stem: Stonehill Audio, a fast-growing firm sells two Dovetail items separately for $50 and $49. A bundle priced 17 percent below the sum of the separate prices would cost how much?
questions.explanation: The separate prices add to $99. A 17 percent discount removes $17, leaving a bundle price of $82. Adding without discounting ignores the promotion, quoting the discount reports the saving rather than the price, and applying the discount twice would overstate the reduction. questions.stem: A Calder Bags, a small firm product in Tarrow is inexpensive, bought frequently and needs no explanation. Which distribution approach fits best?
